analytic.title: RECONFIGURABLE MULTI-CORE SCHEDULING FOR REAL-TIME FUNCTIONS IN AVIONIC MISSION SYSTEMS

div.p: The number and complexity of real-time functions in light and small airsystem's (<25kg) mission systems is steadily increasing. To provide the necessary computational power in a space-restricted environment, Multi-Core processors are used. Today, these Multi-Core processors are statically configured. To utilize the full potential of Multi-Core processors, the step towards dynamically reconfigurable phasedriven Multi-Core configurations has to be taken. In this paper, we will propose an opportunity for reconfigurable phase-driven real-time Multi-Core scheduling resting upon a knowledgebase. Especially we will illustrate the parameters for phase driven real-time tasks, the separation of function sets with mixed real-time requirements during operation, the feasibility and schedulability tests and mainly the creation algorithm of the Knowledgebase.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In avionic mission systems for light and small aircrafts, e.g. micro airsystems, which can be equipped with multiple sensors, a variety of software functions, are implemented in a limited resource environment, with space, power and weight constraints. For example functions to evaluate EOcamera information during an object search or to manage sensor fusion while creating a 3D digital map. However, these functions are strongly dependent on the current aircraft's operational phase (phase-driven), the flight situation or the aircraft configuration. This dependency directly reflects in the computation time of the function. In today's statically configured Multi-Core or Single-Core Software Systems of the aerospace industry, maximum Worst Case Execution Times (WCETs) are reserved for these functions regardless of the airsystem's operational phase and the actual required functions [1]. To utilize a system's limited resource environment more efficiently, the next logical step is to evolve from statically configured Software Systems to reconfigurable Software Systems. The aim of this evolution is to implement more software functions into an embedded control unit or to utilize a less powerful processor.

div.head: Reconfigurable Software Systems
div.p: Reconfigurable Software System functions sets are examined upon their logical dependencies and real-time demands and grouped together in independent, mutually exclusive, logical function sets. During operation, the scheduler dynamically loads the required logical function sets and thus reconfigures the system at runtime. Using this procedure it is possible to temporarily deactivate functions and use the additional free calculation time for different logical function sets. With reference to our initial example, function sets like "object search" or "map creation" outline soft real-time (rt) function sets with several real-time scheduling demands and criticality level (mixed real-time functions). These function sets can be scheduled independently to reach our aim. A scheduler, which supports this procedure of reconfiguration, is the HAMS scheduler.

div.head: HAMS Scheduler
div.p: The HAMS (Hierarchically Asynchronous Multi-Core Scheduler) scheduler consist of a twolayered hierarchical structure [2]. The first layer (FLS) is in charge for managing the tasks on its core while each core in the Multi-Core system has its own FLS entity. Just one entity of the second layer (SLS) is present in the entire Multi-Core System, which is in charge for distributing the functions among the cores. To allocate the functions in a deterministic and 978-1-4799-8940-9/15/$31.00 ©2015 IEEE efficient way the SLS uses a Knowledgebase. The Knowledgebase is a container with configurations for the HAMS scheduler, which specifies the handling, timing, placement, error response and reconfiguration procedure of different phase-driven real-time function sets in the system.

In this paper, we will focus in greater detail on the creation of the Knowledgebase. In the first two chapters, we will deal with the structure of possible avionic real-time functions in a Multi-Core environment and an extension of existing real-time tasks parameters for phase driven systems. The third chapter deals with the segmentation of mixed realtime functions in a running system as well as the schedulability and feasibility tests. In the fourth chapter, the Knowledgebase creation algorithm itself is described. The last chapter deals with a comparison and future possibilities.

Nevertheless, as reconfigurable scheduling is a well-studied subject, attention is paid to related work, e.g. research is done in FPGA based systems [3], in Single-Core hard realtime enviroments [4] as well as in automatic reconfiguration [5].

div.head: Static Real-Time Scheduling
div.p: Two common methods for static rt scheduling are: Clock driven cyclic scheduling or periodic priority driven scheduling [6,7]. In cyclic scheduling periodic hard real-time jobs are only executed in a time slice, which are specifically assigned to them. As time slices and task assignment are statically defined, no dynamic is present in this method of scheduling. Therefore, it is very common in avionics [6]. In priority driven scheduling algorithms the active task with the highest priority is selected to run on the processor by interrupting periodically. A representative of priority scheduling is the Rate Monotonic Scheduling (RMS) algorithm, with static pre assigned priorities [7].

div.head: Reconfigurable Real-Time Scheduling
div.p: Reconfigurable soft real-time scheduling was introduced with the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) Scheduling algorithm. In EDF, the task with the earliest deadline is allowed to execute on the processor while the maximum workload is 100%. If the deadline of a task changes or an aperiodic task is executed, the system becomes highly dynamic and can lead to an unpredictable system behavior in the worst case [8]. In a real-time system where correctness of the result is time-dependent, a shift in task execution can lead to a system breakdown [8]. As a result, the EDF algorithm was further developed into the Maximum Urgency First (MUF) scheduling algorithm [9]. In this algorithm, the same scheduling and feasibility rules as for the EDF algorithm are applied. An additional parameter for "criticality level" has been introduced which should limit the EDF's unpredictable behavior. This parameter takes care that even in a failure case, the task with the highest criticality level should be able to execute.

To bypass the unpredictable behavior of reconfigurable scheduling, it is common practice to use online pre-task admission checks to ensure guaranteed feasibility. Exemplarily two popular approaches are introduced. First of all, an admission control protocol which checks online, by the arrival of the new task, if, alongside with the already to the processor assigned tasks, all tasks can meet their deadline under EDF scheduling [10]. Here tasks reside on the processor and cannot be deleted or migrated, but the time to decide if a new arriving task can be executed on the processor is constant. However, the online admission protocol is not as good as feasibility tests, e.g. Devi's test nor does it deal with changed task parameters. The second approach is an agent-based control algorithm, which tries to transform online the task parameters (deadline, period) which reside on the system in such a way that a new task can be accepted and the system is still feasible [11]. The complexity of the algorithm even rises when Multi-Core processors are used where these online tests may not be applicable in a time-sensitive environment.

In order to reduce the online calculation time and increase performance ratio, our approach is to apply reconfiguration for phase-driven systems by calculating offline the feasibility and schedulability tests for all possible phases. The results are combined in the Knowledgebase, which is the scheduling input for the SLS of the HAMS Scheduler. To the authors' knowledge, no results to this scheme of reconfigurable phase-driven scheduling for function sets with different criticality level and the creation of a knowledgebase are available.

div.head: Tasks in Avionic Mission Systems
div.p: A possible avionic mission system's purpose is, e.g. the creation of a 3D digital map, as it is used in SLAM algorithms (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) [12]. The possible tasks structuring the function set are illustrated in Figure 1. The function set is divided into tasks to run parallel on a Multi-Core processor. In this algorithm, the map creation task is in charge for gathering the sensor data, fusioning them together into a map and sending the results forward to the "Map save" task. Depending on the airsystem and its flight control, it might be possible to actually steer the aircraft, e.g. by sending waypoints (high level commands). The last three named tasks very essential for the airsystem's mission and failures are mission-critical. The "IMU+GPS get Data" and "Laserscanner" tasks gather periodically data to support other functions in their operation.

div.head: Scheduling Requirements
div.p: Figure 1 illustrates a possible map creation algorithm, which consists of three different real-time tasks types.

div.head: • Critical soft real-time periodic tasks
div.p: • Important soft real-time periodic tasks • Important soft real-time aperiodic tasks Critical rt periodic tasks require cyclic scheduling where they are scheduled in a deterministic non interruptible manner. In our map creation example, such task would be the "map creation" and "UAV high level control". Critical periodic rt-tasks have to run independently from all other tasks to execute appropriate measures in a failure case. Cyclic scheduling is the appropriate algorithm for these kinds of tasks. As they are cyclically scheduled, they have to be separate from other functions and the scheduler is in charge for assigned them to the correct time slot and runtime frequency. Important rt periodic task require priority driven scheduling to ensure that the task with the highest priority is always able to calculate and react when lower priority tasks have a failure. Examples for these tasks are the "Laserscanner" and "IMU+GPS get Data" tasks. These tasks support the cyclic task by getting and processing data. They should be independent from external resources like interrupts from the sensor or timer interrupts and prefer polling instead. Important rt aperiodic tasks, like "Get Operator Data", can also be scheduled with priority driven scheduling. However, they consume periodic calculation space even when they are not running if they are not handled separately. A possible solution is to adapt the priority driven scheduling for periodic important tasks to accept aperiodic tasks as well. The "Get Data Operator" function would be a representative. Here the operator can decide on demand to send data or not. Having this set of functions with mixed scheduling requirements it is necessary to redefine the task parameters of rt functions.

div.head: Task Model
div.p: As tasks have different requirements (mixed rt function set), the task model needs to reflect this separation. As a result, the task model for a phase driven system consist of three different parts. First, every scheduling algorithm needs to have the "Basic Task Parameters" as input (I).
div.formula: τ i = ( SC i , {NP a } i , {FP m } i ) (I)
div.p: The SC (Scheduling Class) parameter refers to the scheduling class of the task. As there are three different kinds of rt task in the system the scheduling class can be cyclic scheduling for critical rt task or EDF-periodic scheduling for important periodic or EDF-aperiodic rt tasks. The NP parameter ("Needed Peripherals") is a list of peripherals of the Multi-Core System which are necessary for the task to execute properly, e.g. to communicate with sensors or to manage itself. As in a Multi-Core system not all peripherals might be accessible from every core, this parameter limits the task distribution [13]. The list parameter FP (Function Phases) represents the possible phases of each task and is sub divided into the parameters for each scheduling class:
div.formula: FP m cyclic = (CP m , TP m , DP m , CMP m , S m , R m ) (II)
div.p: In cyclic scheduling for critical rt-tasks the important parameters are CP for Worst Case Execution Time (WCET), TP for the period and DP representing the deadline of the task. These parameters are phase dependent and can reconfigure the scheduling scheme according to the active phase on the system. If the reconfiguration implies a core change, it is possible for the task having a one-time prolonged execution time CMP. This is due to, e.g. data residing on the cache of the prior core that has to be transferred to the new core (cache miss), which prolongs calculation time. The parameters S and R describe the startup sequence of the task in more detail. Where S defines the first time the task is scheduled in the system the parameter R describes after how many times the task has been scheduled and is ready for working according to its definition. The startup procedure has to be examined to this extent, that tasks are not assumed as failures while they are still initializing. The parameters for important rt aperiodic tasks differ in one parameter. The AP parameter expresses the minimum separation time (in this case reaction time) of scheduling the task. This ensures that a task cannot be immediately executed after it has just finished executing and other tasks are allowed to run on the core.

div.head: Mixed Real-Time Scheduling Servers
div.p: Knowing the task structure, the task requirements and the task parameters, the input on how the HAMS scheduler schedules tasks is missing. This input is needed to define the correct Knowledgebase generation algorithm.

div.head: Cyclic Scheduling
div.p: In HAMS cyclic scheduling the start and end of the task is set by the internal clock of the system. The task is ideally not interruptible, excluding non maskable interrupts, and other system related tasks are deferred until to the end. Especially for critical rt periodic task this way of scheduling is preferable, as it ensures the task to get its calculation time independent from other tasks currently running or runnable on the system. For a better common schedulability the tasks periods and deadlines should be harmonic to each other.

div.head: Total Bandwidth Server
div.p: As the cyclic server does not always utilize all calculation time on the processor, the rest can be used for important rt periodic and aperiodic tasks (Figure 2). Therefore, the usage of the HAMS "Total Bandwidth Server" (TBS) is applicable. The TBS is an EDF scheduling server based on the assumption that both periodic and aperiodic tasks can be scheduled in combination. The total utilization can be up to 100% and feasibility can be calculated offline beforehand for known tasks. Thus, this scheduling server makes it ideal for scheduling predefined periodic or aperiodic tasks of reconfigurable software systems as well as scheduling aperiodic unknown OS administration tasks. To detach unknown OS tasks from other tasks their deadline is calculated offline in such a way that the TBS server's total calculation time for one period does not exceed 100% and feasibility is retained. If aperiodic tasks do not arrive within a certain latency the calculation time can be spent on demand for OS tasks.

div.head: Total Bandwidth Server Limitations
div.p: Despite the advantages in comparison to static fixed priority or dynamic scheduling, the usage of mixed real-time scheduling comes along with several limitations:
• Cyclic Server utilization: If the cyclic server has very high utilization the TBS server cannot be established on the core
• Switching costs cyclic to TBS: If there are many cyclic servers on the system the HAMS FLS overhead of switching between scheduling algorithms becomes too expensive
• Switching costs cyclic to cyclic: If the cyclic tasks are not harmonics the switching costs between cyclic tasks becomes too expensive

div.head: Basic Knowledgebase Generation Considerations
div.p: The Knowledgebase generation is split into two different steps. First, the general feasibility and schedulability analyses, which is needed to validate offline the correctness of the task allocation algorithm. Second, the actual offline task distribution to the system's cores with respect to the phase and task requirements.

div.head: Feasibility Tests and Schedulability Algorithms
div.p: As the HAMS scheduler utilizes a cyclic scheduling algorithm in combination with an EDF based TBS the Knowledgebase creation algorithm must acquaint with the altered feasibility tests. Due to the cyclic scheduling algorithms attribute to be nonpreemptable, an overall EDF feasibility and schedulability test cannot be applied, as it requires preemption. Thus, the feasibility tests for the HAMS Knowledgebase have to be divided according to the task allocated on the core.

div.head: Pure Cyclic Scheduling
div.p: In pure cyclic scheduling the feasibility is primarily calculated by getting the major and minor cycle of the actually on the core located tasks. The minor cycle is the greatest common divisor of all tasks periods (T) and the major cycle is the period of the lowest frequent task. Having major and minor cycle the timeslots can be calculated (V).

div.head: (V)
div.p: To test the feasibility of the task set the following formula (VI) can be used.

div.head: (VI)
div.p: In this formula, the calculation time (C) of the task is multiplied by the number of calls (f) within a major cycle and then divided by the period time of the major cycle. This has to be done for all the tasks within a major cycle. If overall utilization is below 100% the set is feasible. However, if the task set is feasible it does not imply schedulability, because in this feasibility test, the deadlines are not considered (or deadlines are set equal to periods). To test schedulability the following algorithm has to be applied (Figure 3).

div.head: Figure 3. Cyclic Server Schedulability Test
div.p: In this algorithm the task set is sorted by the frequency with the highest frequency first and tasks are duplicated according to their frequency. The first task is assigned to every slot of the minor cycle as it is the most frequent task. If the feasibility and deadline tests did not fail, the second task of the task set is assigned to the first minor cycle of every major cycle. If the task does not fit to 100% into the minor slot the task is split into two parts and continued within the next minor cycle. Again, the deadline is checked and the algorithm will continue to place the task as many times into the major cycle as its frequency. This is done until the task set is empty and no deadlines are violated.

div.head: Pure EDF Scheduling Periodic/Aperiodic
div.p: Pure EDF scheduling for phase driven systems is divided into periodic EDF scheduling and a combination of periodic and aperiodic scheduling (TBS). A pure periodic EDF scheduling algorithm will be applied when the utilization maximum is reached, i.e. no other periodic/aperiodic tasks can be allocated on the core and no other aperiodic user or OS task is allowed to interrupt the system. This case makes use of the utilization test by Liu and Layland (LL) [8], which is (VII):

(VII) Whenever the utilization is significantly below 100% a combination of periodic and aperiodic EDF is used. For this case, the feasibility calculation will be divided into two parts. At first, the feasibility for the periodic tasks will be calculated for one period considering the LL test (VII). For aperiodic tasks, the TBS server feasibility calculation will be consulted (VIII) which is the sum of all periodic and aperiodic task utilizations witch all possible repetitions within one period.

div.head: (VIII)
div.p: Additionally we have to test schedulability of the aperiodic tasks according to [6] (IX).

div.head: (IX)
div.p: Here the deadline is calculated for an aperiodic task and the task set is schedulable if the calculated deadline is smaller or equal than the specified deadline D, where r is the percentage of the assigned periodic tasks.

div.head: Cyclic and EDF Scheduling in Combination
div.p: The combination of cycling and EDF based scheduling is deployed when in a major cycle the calculation space between minor cycles is not completely used. The free space can be used to calculate periodic and aperiodic tasks. Checking the feasibility however becomes more difficult because there is no feasibility test for two algorithms. Thus, the feasibility for the two algorithms has to be tested separately. As the cyclic tasks are the first ones to be allocated to the core, the feasibility and schedulability tests as for "pure cyclic scheduling" can be applied. After a successful testing, the free calculation spaces within a major cycle have to be detected. Having done this the EDF feasibility test for periodic tasks is, to sum up the utilization of all periodic tasks that have a period smaller or equal to the major cycle period. The feasibility test is passed if the utilization does not exceed the available calculation space. The schedulability test is to add the periodic tasks to the free slots in respect to their frequency, starting by the most frequent one and check the deadlines to be reached (Figure 4). If there are periodic tasks which have a period greater than the major cycle the feasibility test for this task is: to sum up the free calculation time of the major cycles and minor cycles within the period of the task and compare this to the tasks needed calculation time. The feasibility test again is passed if the utilization does not exceed the available calculation space and schedulability is guaranteed when no deadlines are violated. If there is still free calculation space left and the overall core utilization does not exceed 100% aperiodic tasks can also be assigned to it. However, aperiodic tasks can only be assigned to EDF scheduling section in a minor cycle. Here the feasibility and schedulability can be tested as in normal TBS servers. The minimum separation time (here comparable to reaction time) indicates how often the aperiodic task can and must occur within a major cycle. According to this amount, the task is placed into the according minor cycles and the feasibility, deadline and minimum separation violations are checked. If this test is passed the calculation time is locked for this task at runtime. However, when the task is not runnable at the start of the minor cycles EDF section (e.g. missing operator input) the calculation time is used for OS tasks.

div.head: Offline Task Distribution
div.p: Having the actual feasibility and schedulability tests, the next step is to distribute the tasks among the cores. This has to be done for all tasks that need to run on the system with respect to every different phase a system can be in.

div.head: Bin Packing Algorithms Considerations
div.p: Whenever a certain amount of tasks has to be allocated within limited time and calculation performance on different cores, basic bin packing algorithms can be used. Different bin packing algorithms have been developed and still new algorithms are published [14]. Most known representatives are the FirstFit, NextFit and BestFit algorithms and their derivatives e.g. FirstFit decreasing. However, these algorithms are limited in approximation. Every algorithm has its own performance ratio, which represents the quotient between the optimal solution and the algorithm's solution in the worst-case. This worst-case performance ratio is depending on multiple factors, e.g. the task size. In case of FF decreasing the worstcase performance ratio 11/9 [14]. As it is not acceptable in a system with a limited resource environment to waste resources, i.e. not allocated calculation space, bin packing algorithms for the HAMS scheduler Knowledgebase creation are neglected. A brute force method is used instead to check offline all possible variations of task distribution.

div.head: Pre Task Allocation Algorithm
div.p: A task can be pre allocated to a core if its parameters limit a Multi-Core global allocation. These limiting parameters are:
div.formula: • Peripheral/Interrupt resources • Core lock by user • Task utilization > 95%
div.p: A task, which is depending on a special peripheral component or an interrupt, must be allocated to the core with access to it [13]. As Multi-Core systems can limit the core accessibility to periphery and interrupts tasks must be assigned to the correct core beforehand. The same applies to tasks, which are forced by the user to run only on the specified core. If one task alone is utilizing a core with more than 95% it is best practice to assign a core for its own (single shot scheduling). The overhead of switching between tasks and administration overhead would be too expensive and tasks may not meet there deadline.

div.head: Allocation Algorithm
div.p: At the beginning of the allocation algorithm (Figure 5) the classification of "Logical Function Sets" (LFS) has to be done. Here all logical dependent tasks are grouped together in logical function sets. A LFS can consist of only one task or more tasks. With reference to our initial example, all tasks supporting the "map creation" are one logical function set. All LFS in a system a grouped together to "Dependent Logical Function Sets" (DLFS) when the function sets are mutually exclusive to each other. In the example, the DLFS list consist of the LFS "map create" with all tasks for a map creation and the LFS "object search" containing all tasks to search and identify an object. Afterwards a list of "Independent Logical Function Sets" (ILFS) has to be set up. In ILFS, functions can run independently from each other. When this is done, the bins (B) have to be set up, which is in this case the cores of the Multi-Core processor with their features and access to peripheral components. In the third step, the ILFS has to be examined for limited tasks. If found they are allocated to the bin. If the one bin has a utilization of more than 100% assigned to it, this pre allocation failed and the IFLS is not schedulable. After this, the actual allocation algorithm starts with the following steps: The first is to pick a DLFS from the set of ILFS and lock its phase. All other ILFS are grouped together in a separate list, set to their initial phases and the Bins are cleaned (task_allocation). Secondly, all other ILFS are selected and locked to a specific phase (task_allocation_part2). Thirdly, after all ILFS have been locked to a phase, the critical tasks are allocated to the core and thereby the major and minor cycles are set (allocation_to_bin). Fourthly, the important periodical and afterwards aperiodic tasks are allocated. In the last two steps, it has to be checked if tasks have not already been implemented due to their limitations. The allocation is successful when the feasibility and schedulability tests have been passed. In a while loop the steep two to four are repeated until all phase configurations and possibilities for the ILFS have been allocated. In the next while loop, the phase of the DLFS is changed and again steps two to four are repeated. When all phases of the DLFS are allocated, the next DLFS is taken and again steps one to four are repeated with all other ILFS even if they have been examined before. The algorithm is finished when there is no more DLFS to allocate. Then the set of solutions has to be checked for reconfigurability and double solutions. In the last case, where more than one valid solution is found, the one with the least workload is taken. The complete allocation algorithm was successful when the amount of solution in formula X has been found. Otherwise, no scheduling solution for all phases could be found.

div.head: XML Output Considerations
div.p: After the allocation algorithm has successfully finished the configuration container, a XML file for the HAMS SLS scheduler, is created, also known as the actual Knowledgebase. In this file, the following information has to be inserted for the correct function of the SLS:
• Scheduling type of the core (single shot, pure cyclic, pure EDF, mixed scheduling)
• Duration of the major cycle per core
• Phase of the leading tasks of all LFS
• Start and stop of the cyclic tasks in relation to the major cycle
• Start and stop of the TBS servers also in relation to the major cycle
• Functions belonging the a TBS server and there deadline for EDF scheduling and error recognition
• Times for OS tasks within an TBS server
• A user defined failure task distribution in case of an error

div.head: Results
div.p: For clarification of the prior described algorithms following example of an airsystem's avionic mission system will demonstrate the application.

Two logical function sets, the "map creation set" and the "object search set" should be allocated on the same system. Every set has its own set of sub functions and two complementary phases either "map create" or "object search". The dependency is that either the airsystem can be able to create a map or to search for an object. No function of the two function sets is limited in terms of periphery or by user. The determined function parameters are as shown in Tables 1 and2.

div.head: Comparison and Prospects
div.p: The approach, to use a reconfigurable dynamically scheduled system instead of a statically scheduled system with predefined WCETs shows encouraging results. If the results of our example are compared to statically scheduled system, this system would not be schedulable on a dual core CPU. Instead a tri core has to be implemented (Table 3) with an RMS based scheduler. The next logical step is to compare the TBS server with other dynamic scheduling servers to find the best possible solution for scheduling phase driven systems. When these algorithms are compared and evaluated, they have to be examined in a real runtime environment. Therefore, the Linux kernel is extended with the HAMS scheduler and its FLS and SLS layered structure.
